a1.title: A Man Shares His Tools
a1.excerpt: Tomas has many tools, and now his neighbours can use them for free.
a1.body:
Tomas is 68. He makes tables and chairs. He has a big garage with many tools.

His neighbours buy new tools. But they use them only once. Tomas has an idea. His garage is now a tool library!

People take a tool for one week. It is free. Then Tomas gets the tool again.

Now the library has 300 tools. Every Saturday, people fix old things together. Neighbours are friends now.

The favourite thing is not a tool. It is a chocolate fountain!

a2.title: A Garage Becomes a Free Tool Library
a2.excerpt: A retired carpenter opened his garage to the street, and now 300 tools are free for everyone to borrow.
a2.body:
Tomas is a retired carpenter. He is 68 years old and has a garage full of tools.

Last year, he noticed something. His neighbours often bought new tools. But they only used them once or twice. So Tomas made a free tool library in his garage.

It works like a book library. People borrow a tool for one week, and then they return it. Tomas made library cards from small pieces of wood.

Soon, neighbours gave their old tools to the library. Now there are 300 tools, like drills, ladders and a sewing machine.

Every Saturday morning, people bring broken things, like chairs and lamps. They fix them together. This year, they repaired more than 500 things.

The most popular item is not a tool at all. It's a chocolate fountain!

b1.title: A Retired Carpenter Turns His Garage Into a Tool Library
b1.excerpt: Why buy a drill you'll only use once? One street has found a better answer — and made a lot of new friends along the way.
b1.body:
How many times will you really use a drill? For most people, the answer is “not very often”. That simple question has changed life on one quiet residential street.

Tomas Varga, a 68-year-old retired carpenter, had noticed that his neighbours kept buying expensive tools, using them once and then leaving them in a cupboard. Last year, he decided to try something different. He cleared out his garage, put up some shelves and opened a free tool library.

It works just like a library for books. Neighbours can borrow a tool for up to a week, as long as they bring it back clean. Tomas even carved little wooden library cards for everyone who signs up.

At first, the library had about forty of Tomas's own tools. But once word got around, neighbours started donating theirs. Today the collection has grown to more than 300 items, including ladders, saws, a sewing machine and a pressure washer.

On Saturday mornings, the garage becomes a repair café. People bring broken chairs, lamps and toasters, and fix them together with help from Tomas and other volunteers. So far this year, they have repaired over 500 things that would otherwise have been thrown away.

“I've lived here for thirty years,” one neighbour said, “but I've met more people in this garage than in all that time before.”

The town council is now thinking about opening tool libraries in three more neighbourhoods. And the most borrowed item? Not a tool at all — it's a chocolate fountain.

b2.title: Why Buy a Drill? The Garage Library That Brought a Street Together
b2.excerpt: A retired carpenter's hunch that his neighbours owned too many barely used tools has grown into a 300-item lending library, a weekly repair café and an unexpectedly busy social life.
b2.body:
Most household drills, it is often said, are used for a grand total of about thirteen minutes in their entire lifetime. Whether or not that figure is accurate, it was enough to set Tomas Varga thinking.

The 68-year-old retired carpenter had watched his neighbours buy expensive tools for one-off jobs, only for them to be shoved into cupboards and forgotten. “Every house on this street had the same drill sitting in a box,” he said. “It seemed a bit silly.”

Last year, he decided to do something about it. His garage was cleared, fitted with shelves and reopened as a free tool library. The system is borrowed, quite literally, from the public library: residents can take out a tool for up to seven days, provided it is returned clean and in working order. Each member is issued a small wooden library card, carved by Tomas himself.

The library began with around forty of his own tools. Once word got round, however, donations started pouring in, and the collection now numbers more than 300 items — from ladders and circular saws to a sewing machine and a pressure washer that, according to the booking sheet, is reserved for most of the spring.

On Saturday mornings the garage is transformed into a repair café. Neighbours arrive with wobbly chairs, broken lamps and toasters that have given up, and fix them side by side. More than 500 objects have been repaired this year, most of which would otherwise have ended up in a skip.

Perhaps the biggest change, though, has been social. Several residents said they had lived on the street for decades without knowing the people next door. “If it hadn't been for a borrowed ladder, I'd never have met my best friend on this street,” one admitted.

The town council has taken notice, and officials are now considering funding similar libraries in three other neighbourhoods.

And the single most borrowed item in the collection? Not a tool at all. It is, Tomas reports with some amusement, a chocolate fountain — booked forty times and counting.

c1.title: The Borrowing Street: How a Garage Full of Tools Rebuilt a Neighbourhood
c1.excerpt: Frustrated by the sight of identical, barely used drills in every house on his street, a retired carpenter opened a lending library in his garage — and inadvertently repaired the social fabric of the neighbourhood.
c1.body:
It is one of those statistics that circulates so widely nobody quite remembers where it came from: the average household drill, we are told, is used for about thirteen minutes over its entire lifespan. Tomas Varga has no idea whether the figure is accurate. What he does know is that, until last year, there were at least a dozen of them on his street, most of them still in their original packaging.

The 68-year-old retired carpenter had spent years watching his neighbours purchase expensive equipment for one-off jobs — a shelf here, a fence panel there — only for it to be consigned to the back of a cupboard. “It struck me as faintly absurd,” he says. “Thirty houses, thirty drills, and on any given day perhaps one of them in use.”

His remedy was characteristically practical. Last year he emptied his garage, lined its walls with shelving and reopened it as a free tool library, modelled closely on the public lending system. Members may borrow any item for up to a week, provided it comes back clean and in working order, and each is issued with a small library card that Tomas carves by hand from offcuts of oak.

The initial stock consisted of around forty of his own tools. Once news of the venture spread, however, donations arrived with remarkable speed, and the inventory now exceeds 300 items: ladders, circular saws, a tile cutter, a sewing machine and a pressure washer so heavily in demand that its booking sheet resembles the waiting list for a fashionable restaurant.

On Saturday mornings, the garage takes on a second identity as a repair café. Residents turn up with wobbly chairs, temperamental lamps and toasters that have long since given up, and set about mending them together under Tomas's patient supervision. Over 500 objects have been repaired so far this year, the vast majority of which would otherwise have been destined for landfill.

Remarkably, the whole system runs on trust. There are no deposits and no fines; borrowers simply sign a battered ledger that hangs from a nail by the door. In more than a year of operation, Tomas says, only two items have gone missing — and one of those, a spirit level, was returned three months later with an apologetic note and a jar of homemade marmalade. “People look after things,” he observes, “when they know their neighbours are waiting for them.”

Yet what residents speak about most is not the tools but the conversations they have made possible. Several admit that, for decades, they knew their neighbours only by their cars. “Were it not for a borrowed stepladder, I would never have met the woman who is now my closest friend,” says one, who has lived on the street for nearly thirty years. Children, meanwhile, have become regulars at the Saturday sessions, learning to wield a screwdriver alongside adults they once passed in silence.

The experiment has not gone unnoticed at the town hall. Council officials, who visited in the summer, are now weighing up whether to fund similar libraries in three other neighbourhoods, and Tomas has been invited to advise on how they might be run. His guidance, he says, is refreshingly simple: start small, trust people, and label everything.

There remains one curiosity he has yet to fully explain. The most frequently borrowed item in the entire collection is not a drill, a saw or even the famously oversubscribed pressure washer. It is a chocolate fountain, donated anonymously and booked, at the latest count, forty times. “I don't ask questions,” Tomas says. “A library lends what people need.”
